q: If portions of the building/s are erected at different periods of time, thus increasing the construction period and Architect's burden of services, charges pertaining to services rendered during the Construction Phase-shall be adjusted proportionately. As such, the fee for the remaining works shatibe doubled if the suspension of construction exceeds a period of how many months?
n: Under SPP Doc. 202, if construction is suspended for more than six months, the fee for the remaining works (periodic construction supervision) is doubled. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Manner of Payment (phased construction).

q: What does the acronym PRC stand for?
n: PRC stands for the Professional Regulation Commission. This is the government agency that supervises the licensure boards, including the Professional Regulatory Board of Architecture. Source: RA 8981 (PRC Modernization Act of 2000).

q: A newly passed architect, duly registered with the PRC, shall ___ become a member of the UAP and shall receive the benefits and privileges provided for and described in its by-laws upon payment of required fees and dues.
n: Once registered, an architect automatically becomes a member of the IAPOA (UAP) and receives the benefits in its by-laws upon paying the required fees and dues. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 40.

q: What governs the renewal and issuance of PRC PIC?
n: Issuance and renewal of the Professional Identification Card are governed by the PRC's rules and regulations. Source: RA 8981, Sec. 7; PRC Resolution on PIC renewal.

q: A Registered and Licensed Architect is preparing to renew his Professional Identification Card (PIC). According to the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC), what is the standard validity period of an architect's PRC license before renewal is required?
n: The PRC license (PIC) is valid for three years and must then be renewed, with CPD compliance. Source: RA 8981, Sec. 7(m); PRC Resolution No. 2019-1146 / RA 10912.

q: The government body responsible for regulating the practice of architecture in the Philippines performs several key functions, including preparing the contents of licensure examinations, prescribing and revising course requirements, recommending measures for advancement in the field, inspecting schools, enforcing a Code of Ethics, administering oaths, issuing Certificates of Registration, and investigating or disciplining erring practitioners. These functions are performed by the PRB-ARC. What does this acronym stand for?
n: PRB-ARC (PRBoA) stands for the Professional Regulatory Board of Architecture. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 4 and Sec. 7 (Powers and Functions of the Board).

q: It is the required open space within the interior of the lot, enclosed or partially enclosed by building walls, intended to provide natural light and ventilation to adjacent rooms.
n: A court is an unoccupied open space inside the lot, bounded by building walls and a yard or another court, that provides light and ventilation. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII, Sec. 804 and Glossary (Court).

q: It is the required open space left between the outermost face of the building/structure and the property lines.
n: A yard is the required open space between the outermost face of the building and the property lines. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII, Sec. 804.3.

q: It is the required minimum distance between the outermost face of the building/structure and the property lines.
n: A setback is the required minimum distance, measured at 90°, from the outermost face of the building to the property lines. The width of the yard is the setback. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Glossary (Setback); Rule VIII, Sec. 804.3.

q: In accordance with the National Building Code and its IRR, what is the minimum required front setback for commercial, industrial, institutional, and recreational buildings abutting a 30-meter wide road right-of-way (RROW)?
n: Table VIII.3 requires an 8.00 m front setback for commercial, industrial, institutional and recreational buildings on roads 30.00 m wide or more. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VIII, Table VIII.3.

q: A developer discovers during design development that the proposed building footprint cannot fully comply with the minimum setback requirements imposed by the zoning ordinance. The project is otherwise consistent with the allowable land use and development controls in the area. What is the MOST appropriate course of action?
o: Seek executive approval from the local chief executive based on the project's economic benefits.
Revise the upper floors to project into the setback area provided the ground floor setback is maintained.
Proceed with construction and address any setback deficiencies during permit evaluation.
Apply for a zoning variance or exception through the proper regulatory process.
n: A footprint that cannot meet the setbacks needs a variance or exception through the zoning board's process. Projecting into the setback or building first violates the code. Source: HLURB/DHSUD Model Zoning Ordinance (Variances and Exceptions); NBC Sec. 301.

q: Every corner building on a public street or alley less than 3.6 m in width shall be made with a chaflan. The face of the triangle so formed shall be at right angles to the bisector of the angle of intersection of the street lines. The minimum width of the chaflan shall be how many meters?
n: Corner buildings or solid fences on streets less than 3.60 m wide must be truncated with a chaflan at least 4.00 m long. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule X, Sec. 1008.1.

q: When your vehicle is parked at a space not located on the same lot or property as the principal use it serves.
n: Off-site parking consists of slots located outside the lot or property of the principal use they serve. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Glossary (Off-site Parking).

q: When a building is of mixed occupancy or used for more than one occupancy, the whole building shall be subject to the most restrictive requirement pertaining to any type of occupancy found therein, except where the minor accessory uses do not occupy more than ___ of the area of any floor of a building, nor more than ___ of the basic area permitted in the occupancy requirements, in which case the major use of the building shall determine the occupancy classification.
n: Where minor accessory uses take up no more than 10% of any floor (or of the basic area permitted), the major use sets the occupancy classification. Otherwise the most restrictive requirement applies. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule VII, Sec. 702.b.

q: The PRC Modernization Act is otherwise known as
n: The PRC Modernization Act of 2000 is RA 8981. It reorganized the Professional Regulation Commission and defined its powers over the professional regulatory boards. Source: RA 8981.

q: What is RA 9266
o: National Structural Code of the Philippines
National Plumbing Code of the Philippines
n: RA 9266 is the Architecture Act of 2004. It regulates the practice of architecture in the Philippines and repealed RA 545. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 1.

q: The National Plumbing Code of the Philippines is otherwise known as
n: The National Plumbing Code of the Philippines was enacted as RA 1378 (1955). Its current implementing code is the Revised National Plumbing Code of 1999. Source: RA 1378.

q: A set of standards and regulations that govern the safe and proper installation, operation and maintenance of electrical systems in the Philippines. It ensures the safety and reliability of electrical installations.
n: The Philippine Electrical Code governs the safe installation, operation and maintenance of electrical systems. Source: RA 7920, Sec. 2 (PEC as the governing code).

q: A comprehensive set of regulations governing the design, construction and maintenance of structures in the Philippines that guides structural and civil engineers in designing and assessing buildings and other structures.
n: The National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP) governs structural design, construction and assessment of buildings and other structures. Source: ASEP, NSCP 2015 (7th ed.), Sec. 101.

q: The Fire Code of the Philippines is otherwise known as
n: The Fire Code of the Philippines of 2008 is RA 9514. It repealed PD 1185 and is implemented through the 2019 Revised IRR. Source: RA 9514.

q: Which of the following laws was the original legislation that established fire safety standards in the Philippines before it was repealed and replaced by a more comprehensive fire code in 2008?
n: PD 1185 (1977) was the original Fire Code. RA 9514 (2008) repealed and replaced it. Source: RA 9514, Sec. 14 (repealing clause).

q: Which law, enacted in 2008 to repeal Presidential Decree No. 1185, introduced updated fire safety standards, stricter enforcement mechanisms, and enhanced penalties for violations—thereby becoming the official Revised Fire Code of the Philippines?
n: RA 9514 (2008) repealed PD 1185 and became the Revised Fire Code of the Philippines. Source: RA 9514.

q: Of the following, which has the primary relevance in the management and conservation of forests?
n: PD 705, the Revised Forestry Code (1975), governs the management and conservation of forests. Source: PD 705.

q: Which of the following Presidential Decrees, often misattributed due to overlapping environmental mandates, is officially recognized as the Philippine Environmental Code enacted in 1977?
n: PD 1152 (1977) is the Philippine Environment Code. It sets policies on air and water quality, land use, natural resources and waste management. Source: PD 1152.

q: Which Philippine law formally declared the Philippine Environmental Policy, emphasizing harmony between man and nature, and introduces the requirement for Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) for projects that may significantly affect the environment?
n: PD 1151 (1977) declared the Philippine Environmental Policy and introduced the Environmental Impact Statement requirement. Source: PD 1151, Sec. 4.

q: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence involved in securing an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC)?
o: Project Description → Environmental Impact Assessment → Review and Evaluation → ECC Issuance
Environmental Impact Assessment → Project Description → Review and Evaluation → ECC Issuance
Project Description → Review and Evaluation → Environmental Impact Assessment → ECC Issuance
Project Description → Environmental Impact Assessment → ECC Issuance → Review and Evaluation
n: The ECC process runs: Project Description, then Environmental Impact Assessment (EIS/IEE), then review and evaluation by the DENR-EMB, then ECC issuance. Source: DAO 2003-30 (IRR of PD 1586), EIA process.

q: A developer proposes a large-scale project within an environmentally sensitive area. As part of the ECC application process, the DENR-EMB requires a comprehensive document that analyzes the proposed development, evaluates alternatives, identifies potential environmental consequences, and prescribes mitigation and monitoring measures. What document is being required?
n: For projects in environmentally critical areas, the EMB requires an Environmental Impact Statement. It analyzes the project and alternatives, predicts impacts, and sets mitigation and monitoring measures. Source: PD 1586; DAO 2003-30.

q: Under the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) System, what is the primary purpose of securing an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC)?
o: To formally approve the Environmental Impact Statement and authorize the immediate commencement of construction activities.
To certify that the proposed project has been reviewed and found environmentally acceptable, provided that the proponent complies with the specified environmental management and monitoring measures.
To confirm that the Environmental Impact Assessment has identified all potential environmental impacts and that no further environmental obligations will be required from the project proponent.
To certify that the Project Description submitted by the proponent is complete and acceptable for filing.
n: An ECC certifies that the project was reviewed and found environmentally acceptable, provided the proponent complies with the stated management and monitoring conditions. Source: PD 1586; DAO 2003-30, Sec. 3 (definition of ECC).

q: A developer proposes a resort project within an environmentally sensitive coastal area. Before the DENR-EMB can determine the project's environmental acceptability and issue an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC), which document is primarily intended to identify, predict, and evaluate the project's significant environmental impacts and propose measures to mitigate them?
n: The Environmental Impact Assessment identifies, predicts and evaluates a project's significant impacts and proposes mitigation, before the EMB decides on the ECC. Source: DAO 2003-30, Sec. 3 (definition of EIA).

q: Under the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) System, which statement BEST distinguishes an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) from an Initial Environmental Examination (IEE)?
o: An EIS is submitted only for government projects, while an IEE is submitted only for private-sector projects.
An EIS results in the issuance of an ECC, while an IEE results in the issuance of a Building Permit.
An EIS is prepared only after an ECC has been issued. while an IEE is prepared prior to ECC application.
An EIS is intended for projects with potentially significant environmental impacts, while an IEE is generally used for projects with less significant or more predictable environmental effects.
n: An EIS is for projects with potentially significant impacts. An IEE is a simpler study for projects with less significant or more predictable effects. Source: DAO 2003-30 (EIS vs. IEE).

q: Which Philippine law specifically prescribes alternative technical standards for economic and socialized housing projects, including reduced road right-of-way widths and minimum lot sizes?
n: BP 220 sets alternative technical standards for economic and socialized housing, including reduced road widths and lot sizes. Source: BP 220 and its Revised IRR.

q: Which Philippine law governs medium-cost and open market housing developments, including subdivisions and condominiums intended for middle- to upper-income buyers, and sets standards for lot sizes, setbacks, open space allocation, and buyer protection?
n: PD 957 governs open-market and medium-cost subdivisions and condominiums, setting design standards and protecting buyers. Source: PD 957 and its Revised IRR (2008).

q: Which Philippine law, known as the "Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992," mandates the Balanced Housing Development Program, empowers local government units to implement housing projects, promotes rational land use, and covers all lands in urban and urbanizable zones including resettlement areas?
n: RA 7279 is the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992. It mandates the Balanced Housing Development Program. Source: RA 7279, Secs. 1 and 18.

q: Which Republic Act governs the policies, procedures, and guidelines for the procurement of goods, infrastructure projects, and consulting services by all branches of government, including architectural services in the Philippines?
n: RA 9184, the Government Procurement Reform Act, governs government procurement of goods, infrastructure and consulting services, including architectural services. Since 2024 it has been superseded by RA 12009 (New Government Procurement Act). Source: RA 9184; RA 12009.

q: Which Philippine law, officially titled "An Act to Institutionalize the Use of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) in the Philippines and to Establish the Office for Alternative Dispute Resolution," provides the legal framework for resolving architectural and construction-related disputes through non-litigious venues such as mediation, arbitration, and conciliation—often administered by bodies like the CIAC or the Office for Alternative Dispute Resolution (OADR)?
n: RA 9285, the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 2004, institutionalizes ADR and created the Office for Alternative Dispute Resolution. Source: RA 9285.

q: Disputes between project owners, contractors, subcontractors, and consultants may be resolved through a specialized government body that handles arbitration and mediation for construction-related conflicts. This body was created to provide a faster, industry-focused alternative to regular courts. What does the acronym CIAC stand for?
o: Council for Infrastructure Arbitration and Compliance
n: CIAC stands for the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission. EO 1008 (1985) created it to arbitrate construction disputes. Source: EO 1008 (Construction Industry Arbitration Law).

q: Which type of construction cost refers to the direct, tangible expenses associated with building a structure, such as labor, materials, equipment, and site work?
n: Hard costs are the direct, tangible costs of building: labor, materials, equipment and site work. Source: Construction cost-estimating practice; 2016 Architect's Guidelines (PCC definition).

q: Which type of construction cost refers to indirect, non-physical expenses such as architectural fees, permits, insurance, and financing charges that support the completion of a project but are not part of the actual building work?
n: Soft costs are indirect, non-physical costs such as professional fees, permits, insurance and financing. Source: Construction cost-estimating practice; 2016 Architect's Guidelines (PDC definition).

q: Which term refers to the total sum that includes construction cost, professional fees, permits, clearances, utilities, cost of acquiring the project site or lot, and cost of money?
n: Project Development Cost is the total of construction cost, professional fees, permits and clearances, utilities, land acquisition and cost of money. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Definitions (Project Development Cost).

q: In the context of architectural compensation under the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), which financial metric serves as the exclusive basis for computing the architect's Basic Fee, and excludes land acquisition, professional fees, permits, utilities, and financing costs?
n: The architect's fee is computed on Project Construction Cost. It excludes land, professional fees, permits, utilities and financing. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Definitions (Project Construction Cost).

q: An architect enters into a design contract with a client, later discovers a conflict of interest involving a related party, and chooses to withdraw from the project to preserve professional integrity. The client insists that the architect is legally bound to continue under the terms of the agreement. In resolving this dispute, which document primarily governs the architect's obligation to act with honesty, fairness, and professional decorum—even when such action may contradict contractual expectations?
o: Code of Ethical Conduct for Architects issued by the PRBoA and PRC
Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) under the IRR of R.A. No. 9266
Civil Code of the Philippines – Book IV on Obligations and Contracts
n: An architect's duty to act with honesty, fairness and professional decorum, even against contractual expectations, comes from the Code of Ethical Conduct issued by the PRBoA and PRC. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct); RA 9266, Sec. 7(f).

q: Which term best describes the foundational discipline that involves the systematic measurement and analysis of human body dimensions, used to inform spatial configurations, circulation paths, and ergonomic relationships between users and built environments?
n: Anthropometry is the systematic measurement of human body dimensions. It informs space sizes, circulation and ergonomics. Source: Panero & Zelnik, Human Dimension and Interior Space (1979).

q: A client insists on proceeding with construction without securing a Building Permit and asks the architect to continue the project. Under the Code of Ethics for Filipino Architects, which ethical provision would the architect violate if he agrees to the client's request?
o: The architect's obligation to avoid unfair competition with other architects
The architect's duty to maintain confidentiality of client information
The architect's obligation to give proper credit to collaborators and consultants
The architect's responsibility to protect public health, safety, and welfare
n: Building without a permit puts public safety at risk and breaks the law. Going along with it breaches the architect's duty to protect public health, safety and welfare. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct) (Responsibility to the Public); NBC Sec. 301.

q: The owner instructs the Architect-in-Charge of Construction (AICC) to change the specified materials to cheaper alternatives. The AICC agrees and implements the change without informing the Architect-of-Record (AOR). Which specific ethical duty under the Code of Ethical Conduct is violated?
o: Responsibility to the Client – avoiding conflict of interest
Responsibility to the Public – ensuring safety and welfare
Responsibility to the Profession – interfering with or altering another architect's work without consent
Responsibility to the Client – safeguarding the client's financial interest
n: Changing another architect's specified work without his knowledge or consent breaches the duty to fellow architects under Responsibility to the Profession. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct) (Responsibility to Colleagues/Profession).

q: An architect hires newly licensed architects at below minimum wage and requires extended working hours to "save on expenses and be competitive," justifying it by saying that this is normal and expected for starting architects. Which ethical duty is violated?
o: No violation, as this is standard practice
n: Underpaying and overworking young architects to undercut competitors violates the Responsibility to the Profession, which includes fair treatment and compensation of fellow architects and staff. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct) (Responsibility to the Profession and to Colleagues).
